reactions.observation_en: The white zinc oxide powder dissolves in the acid. Solution clears. Mild warming.
reactions.explanation_en: ZnO is an amphoteric oxide that reacts with both acids and bases. With H₂SO₄, the oxide acts as a base, neutralizing the acid to form zinc sulfate and water. ZnO dissolves because the ionic Zn²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are soluble.
reactions.condition_notes: Slight warming helps. Acidic medium. ZnO is amphoteric (also dissolves in NaOH).
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Wear gloves and work in fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The dark green Cr₂O₃ slowly dissolves. Solution turns dark green as CrCl₃ forms.
reactions.explanation_en: Chromium(III) oxide is amphoteric but dissolves in strong acids. The Cr³⁺ ions in solution give a characteristic dark green color as chromium(III) chloride. Heating is needed because Cr₂O₃ has a very stable crystal structure.
reactions.condition_notes: Needs heating (~60°C). Acidic medium. Cr₂O₃ is very refractory (hard to dissolve). Used as a green pigment.
reactions.safety_notes: Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Health hazard — prolonged exposure risk. Fume hood required.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The dark yellow-brown FeCl₃ solution rapidly decolorizes. Dark iron particles deposit. Significant heat released.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium is much higher than iron in the activity series. Mg atoms lose 2 electrons each, reducing Fe³⁺ to metallic iron. The very large difference in reactivity makes this reaction vigorous and highly exothermic.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Very exothermic due to large reactivity gap. Clean Mg surface for best results.
reactions.safety_notes: Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: Brilliant white sparks and intense white-yellow light. Molten iron droplets form. Temperature exceeds 2500°C. Blinding flash.
reactions.explanation_en: The thermite reaction is one of the most exothermic reactions known. Aluminum reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron while being oxidized to aluminum oxide. The reaction produces temperatures above 2500°C, sufficient to melt iron. Used for welding railroad tracks.
reactions.condition_notes: Very high ignition temperature (~900°C, typically using a magnesium ribbon). Once started, self-sustaining. Cannot be extinguished with water.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Extreme heat hazard — risk of burns. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982; NIST-JANAF 1998

reactions.observation_en: Very vigorous bubbling and effervescence. Magnesium ribbon dissolves rapidly. Solution heats up significantly.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium is high in the reactivity series and reacts vigorously with dilute sulfuric acid. Mg is oxidized to Mg²⁺ while H⁺ is reduced to H₂ gas. The reaction is strongly exothermic and proceeds rapidly.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Very vigorous — add Mg slowly. H₂ pop test can be performed.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

reactions.name_en: Copper Sulfate and Ammonia (Complex Ion Formation)

warnings_en: Cu compounds are harmful if ingested.

reactions.observation_en: First a pale blue Cu(OH)₂ precipitate forms with a little NH₃, then with excess NH₃ it dissolves to give a deep royal blue solution of [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
reactions.explanation_en: Ammonia acts as a ligand, donating its lone pair to Cu²⁺ to form the tetraamminecopper(II) complex [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. The deep blue color is diagnostic and much more intense than the pale blue of hydrated Cu²⁺. This demonstrates ligand field theory and d–d transitions.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Basic medium (excess NH₃). First add small amount of NH₃ to see Cu(OH)₂ precipitate, then add excess to dissolve it.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Fume hood required.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for Cu(NH3)4SO4(aq)

reactions.observation_en: Intense blood-red color appears instantly upon mixing. Even trace amounts of Fe³⁺ produce visible color. Classic test for iron(III) ions.
reactions.explanation_en: Fe³⁺ ions react with SCN⁻ to form the intensely colored [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ complex. The blood-red color is due to charge transfer between Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻. This reaction is so sensitive it can detect Fe³⁺ at parts-per-million concentrations.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Extremely sensitive test. The equilibrium can be shifted by adding more Fe³⁺ or SCN⁻ (Le Chatelier’s principle demonstration).
reactions.safety_notes: Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for Fe(SCN)Cl2(aq)

reactions.observation_en: Shiny reddish copper surface gradually darkens to black CuO when heated in air. The oxide layer forms progressively.
reactions.explanation_en: Copper reacts with oxygen when heated to form black copper(II) oxide. At lower temperatures, red Cu₂O (copper(I) oxide) forms first, then further oxidation produces black CuO. This is much slower than iron rusting because the CuO layer partially protects the underlying metal.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires heating (~200°C). Unlike iron rust, copper oxide is somewhat protective. Green patina on copper is a different process (reacting with CO₂ and moisture).
reactions.safety_notes: Heating required — use heat-resistant glassware.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The black CuO powder gradually turns reddish-brown as metallic copper forms. The mixture glows when heated. CO₂ gas is released.
reactions.explanation_en: Carbon is a stronger reducing agent than copper at high temperatures. Carbon is oxidized to CO₂ while Cu²⁺ in CuO is reduced to metallic copper. This demonstrates the principle of smelting — extracting metals from their ores using carbon.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires heating to ~400°C. Classic school demonstration of metal extraction by reduction. Mix CuO and charcoal powder thoroughly.
reactions.safety_notes: Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Significant heat release — handle with caution. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.name_en: Carbon Reduction of Iron Oxide (Blast Furnace)
reactions.observation_en: At high temperature, the red-brown iron oxide converts to grey metallic iron. CO₂ gas is released. In a blast furnace, molten iron collects at the bottom.
reactions.explanation_en: This is the industrial process for iron production (simplified). Carbon (as coke) reduces iron(III) oxide to metallic iron. At blast furnace temperatures (~1500°C), the actual reducing agent is CO formed from C + CO₂. This process has been used for over 3000 years.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires very high temperature (~700°C in lab, ~1500°C in blast furnace). The foundation of the Iron Age and modern steel industry.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Significant heat release — handle with caution. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: H₂ gas is flammable and explosive.
Purge apparatus with H₂ before heating.

reactions.observation_en: Black CuO turns shiny pink-orange as metallic copper forms. Water droplets condense on cool surfaces downstream.
reactions.explanation_en: Hydrogen gas reduces copper(II) oxide to metallic copper while being oxidized to water. This is a clean reduction producing only water as a byproduct. H₂ is the reducing agent, gaining oxygen from CuO.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires ~300°C. CRITICAL: purge apparatus with H₂ before heating to avoid explosion of H₂–air mixture. Classic reduction demonstration.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Causes deep tissue burns without immediate pain.

reactions.observation_en: No visible change. The solution warms slightly. HF is a weak acid despite its extreme danger to tissue.
reactions.explanation_en: HF is a weak acid (Ka = 6.8 × 10⁻⁴) due to the very strong H–F bond. However, it is extremely dangerous because fluoride ions penetrate tissue and bind calcium, causing deep burns and potentially fatal hypocalcemia. The neutralization with NaOH makes it safer.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. HF is a weak acid but EXTREMELY hazardous. This reaction is used for safe disposal of HF waste.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Toxic — handle with extreme care.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: HBr is corrosive and produces irritating fumes.

reactions.observation_en: Clear solution remains. Noticeable heat release. No precipitate or gas evolution.
reactions.explanation_en: HBr is a strong acid that fully dissociates in water. It donates H⁺ to OH⁻ from KOH, forming water. K⁺ and Br⁻ ions remain dissolved as potassium bromide. KBr was historically used as a sedative in medicine.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Strong acid–strong base neutralization. Fully exothermic.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Can cause fires with combustible materials.

reactions.observation_en: Purple crystals darken and melt, then release oxygen gas which can relight a glowing splint. Brown-black MnO₂ residue remains.
reactions.explanation_en: Potassium permanganate decomposes when heated, releasing oxygen gas. The Mn is reduced from +7 (in MnO₄⁻) to +4 (in MnO₂). The released O₂ can be tested with a glowing splint, which relights in the oxygen-rich atmosphere.
reactions.condition_notes: Needs heating to ~240°C. O₂ collection possible. The glowing splint test confirms oxygen evolution.
reactions.safety_notes: Oxidizer — do not mix with combustibles. Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. Heating required — use heat-resistant glassware.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for K2MnO4(s)

warnings_en: Do not mix with combustible materials.

reactions.observation_en: White crystals melt and decompose. Oxygen gas released can relight a glowing splint. Residue is potassium nitrite (KNO₂).
reactions.explanation_en: Potassium nitrate decomposes on heating, with the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) losing one oxygen atom to become nitrite (NO₂⁻). The released oxygen supports combustion. KNO₃ is saltpeter — the oxidizer in traditional gunpowder.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires ~400°C. KNO₃ is the oxidizer in fireworks and gunpowder. The oxygen-rich decomposition enables rapid combustion of fuels.
reactions.safety_notes: Oxidizer — do not mix with combustibles. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The white ZnO powder dissolves in the NaOH solution to form a clear zincate solution.
reactions.explanation_en: Zinc oxide is amphoteric, meaning it reacts with both acids and bases. With NaOH, ZnO acts as an acidic oxide, forming sodium zincate (Na₂ZnO₂). This dual behavior is characteristic of elements near the metal–nonmetal boundary.
reactions.condition_notes: Slightly above room temperature. Basic medium. Demonstrates amphoteric behavior of ZnO. Compare with ZnO + H₂SO₄.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for Na2ZnO2(aq)

reactions.observation_en: Slow bubbling as hydrogen evolves. Tin dissolves gradually. Solution of tin(II) chloride forms.
reactions.explanation_en: Tin is above hydrogen in the activity series but only slightly, so the reaction is slow. Sn is oxidized to Sn²⁺ while H⁺ is reduced to H₂ gas. Heating accelerates the dissolution. Tin chloride (SnCl₂) is soluble.
reactions.condition_notes: Needs warming to ~50°C. Acidic medium. Slow reaction — compare with Zn + HCl which is much faster.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Reaction can be vigorous when hot.

reactions.observation_en: Bubbling as hydrogen gas evolves. Aluminum foil dissolves. Solution may foam. Reaction speeds up as it heats itself.
reactions.explanation_en: Unlike most metals, aluminum reacts with strong bases as well as acids (amphoteric behavior). NaOH dissolves the protective Al₂O₃ layer, then Al reduces water to H₂ while being oxidized to aluminate ions [Al(OH)₄]⁻. Never clean aluminum with oven cleaner (NaOH-based).
reactions.condition_notes: Needs warming to ~50°C to start. Basic medium. Self-accelerating as exothermic. Demonstrates amphoteric nature of aluminum.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable — keep away from ignition sources. Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: SiO₂ dust is hazardous to lungs.

reactions.observation_en: SiO₂ slowly dissolves in concentrated NaOH at high temperature, forming a clear sodium silicate solution (water glass).
reactions.explanation_en: SiO₂ is an acidic oxide with an extremely stable covalent network structure. It reacts with strong bases at high temperatures to form sodium silicate (Na₂SiO₃, known as water glass). This is why NaOH is stored in plastic, not glass bottles.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires very high temperature or prolonged heating with concentrated NaOH. This is why NaOH etches glass and must be stored in plastic containers.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. High ignition temperature — specialized equipment needed.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for Na2SiO3(aq)

reactions.observation_en: A bright yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI) forms immediately. Very distinctive canary yellow color.
reactions.explanation_en: Ag⁺ combines with I⁻ to form AgI, which is even less soluble than AgCl or AgBr (Ksp ≈ 8.5 × 10⁻¹⁷). The yellow color distinguishes it from white AgCl and pale yellow AgBr. AgI is used in cloud seeding to promote rain formation.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. AgI is the least soluble silver halide. Color comparison: AgCl (white) < AgBr (pale yellow) < AgI (bright yellow).
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Environmental hazard — dispose properly.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: With catalyst (KI or MnO₂), rapid foaming and oxygen evolution. With KI + dish soap, creates dramatic elephant toothpaste foam column.
reactions.explanation_en: H₂O₂ is thermodynamically unstable and decomposes to water and oxygen. Without catalyst, this is extremely slow. KI or MnO₂ catalysts dramatically speed the decomposition. The elephant toothpaste demo adds dish soap to trap O₂ in foam, creating a spectacular eruption.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature with catalyst. Without catalyst, very slow. KI or MnO₂ as catalyst. Add dish soap and food coloring for the famous demonstration.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: CO₂ in high concentration displaces oxygen.
H₂CO₃ is a weak acid, safe.

reactions.observation_en: CO₂ dissolves in water with slight fizzing. The resulting solution is slightly acidic (pH ~5.6). This is what makes carbonated water.
reactions.explanation_en: CO₂ is an acidic oxide that dissolves in water to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), a weak diprotic acid. Only a small fraction of dissolved CO₂ actually forms H₂CO₃ (about 0.3%). This reaction is responsible for the acidity of rainwater and carbonated beverages.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Higher pressure increases CO₂ solubility (carbonation). This is why rain is naturally slightly acidic (pH ~5.6).
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The colorless KBr solution turns orange-brown as bromine (Br₂) is liberated by the more reactive chlorine.
reactions.explanation_en: Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine and a stronger oxidizing agent. Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ from KBr solution, oxidizing Br⁻ to Br₂ (orange-brown) while Cl₂ is reduced to Cl⁻. This demonstrates halogen reactivity order: F > Cl > Br > I.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Classic halogen displacement series. Add organic solvent to extract Br₂ layer for clearer color observation.
reactions.safety_notes: Toxic — handle with extreme care. Environmental hazard — dispose properly. Fume hood required.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The orange bromine solution decolorizes as brown iodine appears. Adding starch indicator turns the solution blue-black (iodine test).
reactions.explanation_en: Bromine is more reactive than iodine in the halogen series. Br₂ oxidizes I⁻ to I₂ while being reduced to Br⁻. The iodine can be confirmed with starch indicator (blue-black color). This completes the halogen displacement series.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Continue the halogen displacement pattern: Cl₂ displaces Br⁻, Br₂ displaces I⁻. Use starch to confirm I₂.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Toxic — handle with extreme care. Fume hood required.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: NH₃ gas is irritating and pungent.

reactions.observation_en: The mixture becomes very cold (can freeze water on the outside of the beaker). Strong ammonia smell. The beaker frosts over.
reactions.explanation_en: This is one of the most dramatic endothermic reactions. Mixing two solids absorbs so much heat that the temperature drops to about −20°C. The reaction produces ammonia gas (pungent smell) and barium chloride. The extreme cooling can freeze a wet board to the beaker.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature. Extremely endothermic. Temperature drop of ~50°C possible. Classic demonstration of endothermic process.
reactions.safety_notes: Corrosive — wear gloves and eye protection. Irritant — avoid skin and eye contact. Extreme cold — risk of frostbite on container. Gas evolved — ensure adequate ventilation. Fume hood required.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Highly corrosive — concentrated nitric acid causes severe burns.
Releases toxic NO2 (reddish-brown) gas — fume hood mandatory.
Strongly exothermic — temperature can spike beyond 80 °C.
Wear gloves, goggles, and a lab coat at all times.

reactions.observation_en: Copper metal vigorously dissolves into the concentrated nitric acid. The solution rapidly turns deep cyan/blue from Cu²⁺ ions, while a thick reddish-brown cloud of NO2 gas rises from the surface. The vessel becomes hot to the touch within seconds.
reactions.explanation_en: Concentrated HNO3 oxidizes copper to Cu²⁺ while nitrogen is reduced from +5 (in NO3⁻) to +4 (in NO2). The full balanced equation is Cu + 4 HNO3 → Cu(NO3)2 + 2 NO2 + 2 H2O. The blue color is from the hexaaquacopper(II) complex; the reddish-brown gas is nitrogen dioxide. The reaction is strongly exothermic (~ΔH = −300 kJ/mol Cu).
reactions.condition_notes: Use concentrated (≥ 8 M) HNO3 at room temperature. Reaction is self-accelerating because of the heat released. Stir gently. Always perform inside a fume hood.
reactions.safety_notes: Highly corrosive and toxic gas. Fume hood required. Strongly exothermic — never scale up beyond a few mL.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: Bubbles of hydrogen gas form at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
reactions.explanation_en: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen gas by an electric current. 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires electrical current. Add electrolyte (e.g. H2SO4) to increase conductivity.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen is flammable - keep away from open flames.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

reactions.observation_en: Ozone gas slowly converts to oxygen gas. The pale blue color fades.
reactions.explanation_en: Ozone (O3) is unstable and decomposes into diatomic oxygen (O2). Chlorine atoms from CFCs catalyze this reaction in the stratosphere.
reactions.condition_notes: Accelerated by UV light and certain catalysts like chlorine.
reactions.safety_notes: Ozone is toxic - ensure proper fume extraction.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Heat hazard. Use tongs and heat-proof mat.

reactions.observation_en: The green powder turns black as copper oxide forms, and CO2 gas is released.
reactions.explanation_en: Copper carbonate decomposes when heated, forming black copper oxide and carbon dioxide gas. CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires strong heating (~200C). Green to black color change is diagnostic.
reactions.safety_notes: Hot apparatus - allow to cool before handling.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for CuCO3(s)

reactions.observation_en: A fruity, sweet smell of ethyl acetate (banana-like) is produced.
reactions.explanation_en: Acetic acid and ethanol react in the presence of an acid catalyst to form ethyl acetate (ester) and water. CH3COOH + C2H5OH -> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires acid catalyst (usually H2SO4) and gentle heating. The ester has a characteristic fruity smell.
reactions.safety_notes: Flammable organic compounds. No open flames near ethanol.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982; NIST Chemistry WebBook

reactions.observation_en: After a short delay, the solution suddenly turns deep blue-black as iodine forms and reacts with starch.
reactions.explanation_en: A classic clock reaction. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes iodide to iodine in acidic conditions. Iodine forms a blue complex with starch.
reactions.condition_notes: Famous demonstration of reaction kinetics. The delay depends on concentration and temperature.
reactions.safety_notes: Iodine stains - wear gloves and protective clothing.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: White sugar turns golden brown then black as it decomposes. Water vapor and caramel aroma are released.
reactions.explanation_en: When heated above its melting point, sucrose decomposes through caramelization, breaking down into carbon and water. C12H22O11 -> 12C + 11H2O.
reactions.condition_notes: Concentrated H2SO4 catalyzes this reaction at room temperature (dehydration of sugar).
reactions.safety_notes: Extremely hot molten sugar causes severe burns - use tongs and heat shield.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NIST Chemistry WebBook

reactions.observation_en: The colorless solution instantly turns bright pink when base is added.
reactions.explanation_en: Phenolpthalein is a pH indicator that is colorless in acidic/neutral solutions and pink in basic solutions (pH > 8.3).
reactions.condition_notes: A classic acid-base indicator. Reversible - adding acid returns the colorless form.
reactions.enthalpyMissing: no sourced standard enthalpy of formation for C20H14O4(aq), C20H12Na2O4(aq)

reactions.observation_en: A colorless gas (ethene) is evolved. The solution darkens as the acid dehydrates the alcohol.
reactions.explanation_en: Ethanol is dehydrated by concentrated sulfuric acid at 170°C to form ethene (ethylene), an alkene. C2H5OH -> C2H4 + H2O. This is an elimination reaction.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires concentrated H2SO4 catalyst and high temperature (170°C). At lower temperatures (140°C), diethyl ether forms instead.
reactions.safety_notes: Concentrated acid is extremely corrosive. Ethene is highly flammable.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: Ethene gas is absorbed into the acidic solution, producing ethanol.
reactions.explanation_en: Ethene gas reacts with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst at 300°C and high pressure to form ethanol. C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH. Industrial method for ethanol production.
reactions.condition_notes: Industrial process: 300°C, 70 atm, H3PO4 catalyst on silica support.
reactions.safety_notes: High pressure and temperature. Industrial scale only.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Bromine is highly toxic and corrosive.

reactions.observation_en: The reddish-brown bromine water rapidly decolorizes as it adds across the double bond. A colorless dibromoethane liquid forms.
reactions.explanation_en: Bromine adds across the carbon-carbon double bond of ethene in an electrophilic addition reaction. The brown color of bromine disappears, confirming the presence of unsaturation. C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2 (1,2-dibromoethane).
reactions.condition_notes: Classic test for unsaturation. Rapid at room temperature. Bromine water decolorization confirms C=C double bond.
reactions.safety_notes: Bromine is HIGHLY TOXIC and corrosive. Must be handled in a fume hood with proper PPE.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The greenish-yellow chlorine color fades as the reaction proceeds. HCl gas (white fumes with ammonia) is detected.
reactions.explanation_en: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of UV light via a free radical substitution mechanism. A hydrogen atom is replaced by chlorine. CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl. Further substitution can produce CH2Cl2, CHCl3, and CCl4.
reactions.condition_notes: Requires UV light or high temperature to initiate free radical chain reaction. Product is a mixture of chloromethanes.
reactions.safety_notes: Toxic gases — perform in fume hood only. UV light can damage eyes.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The ester layer gradually disappears as it hydrolyzes. The fruity smell of ethyl acetate fades and ethanol odor appears.
reactions.explanation_en: Esters undergo alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) to form a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. The reverse of esterification. CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + C2H5OH.
reactions.condition_notes: Proceeds faster with heating. NaOH provides OH- nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon.
reactions.safety_notes: Base is corrosive. Avoid contact with eyes and skin.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982; NIST Chemistry WebBook

reactions.observation_en: A white waxy solid (polyethene) forms as ethene gas polymerizes. The reaction is exothermic and the mixture thickens.
reactions.explanation_en: Ethene monomers join together in a chain reaction to form polyethene (polyethylene), the most common plastic. n(CH2=CH2) -> -(CH2-CH2)n-. Requires initiator and high pressure or Ziegler-Natta catalyst.
reactions.condition_notes: Industrial process: high pressure (1000-3000 atm) or Ziegler-Natta catalyst at lower pressure.

reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: Hot copper glows in sulfur vapor and turns into a brittle blue-black solid.
reactions.explanation_en: With sulfur, a mild oxidizing agent, copper is oxidized only to the +1 state, giving copper(I) sulfide.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.

reactions.observation_en: The mixture burns with a dazzling white flash, leaving a white-grey solid.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium transfers two electrons to sulfur to form ionic magnesium sulfide.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The mixture burns with an intense white glow, leaving a grey solid that smells of rotten eggs in moist air.
reactions.explanation_en: Aluminium sulfide forms very exothermically. It is hydrolyzed by moisture to Al(OH)₃ and H₂S.
reactions.safety_notes: Aluminium powder is flammable. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.

reactions.observation_en: Burning magnesium keeps burning in nitrogen, leaving a greenish-yellow powder.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium is reactive enough to break the very strong N≡N bond and form magnesium nitride. This is why some nitride forms when magnesium burns in air.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Lithium reacts with water and burns fiercely.

reactions.observation_en: The shiny metal slowly becomes covered with a dark red-black crust.
reactions.explanation_en: Lithium is the only alkali metal that reacts with nitrogen at room temperature, forming lithium nitride. The small Li⁺ ion gives a very stable lattice with N³⁻.
reactions.safety_notes: Lithium reacts with water and burns fiercely.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Bromine is toxic and corrosive; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: After a short delay the foil bursts into flame with bright sparks and clouds of orange-brown fumes.
reactions.explanation_en: Once bromine gets through the oxide film, aluminium is oxidized violently to aluminium bromide.
reactions.safety_notes: Aluminium powder is flammable. Bromine is toxic and corrosive; use a fume hood. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Iodine is harmful and stains skin.

reactions.observation_en: A drop of water starts the reaction: the mixture flares up and clouds of purple iodine vapor billow out.
reactions.explanation_en: Aluminium is oxidized by iodine to aluminium iodide. The water drop is the catalyst; the heat released sublimes excess iodine into a purple vapor.
reactions.condition_notes: Room temperature; started by one drop of water as catalyst.
reactions.safety_notes: Aluminium powder is flammable. Iodine is harmful and stains skin.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Iodine is harmful and stains skin.

reactions.observation_en: In a little water the brown iodine color fades as the mixture warms, leaving a colorless solution.
reactions.explanation_en: Zinc reduces iodine to iodide and is oxidized to Zn²⁺, giving soluble zinc iodide. Electrolysis of the solution reverses the reaction.
reactions.safety_notes: Zinc powder is flammable. Iodine is harmful and stains skin.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.
Bromine is toxic and corrosive; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The orange-brown color of bromine fades as the magnesium reacts, and the mixture becomes hot.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium gives two electrons to bromine, forming ionic magnesium bromide.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Bromine is toxic and corrosive; use a fume hood.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.

reactions.observation_en: Burning magnesium keeps burning inside CO₂ with a crackling white flame, leaving white ash with black specks of carbon.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium is such a strong reducing agent that it takes oxygen from CO₂, leaving carbon. This is why CO₂ extinguishers must not be used on metal fires.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.
Do not inhale fine silica dust.

reactions.observation_en: On strong heating the mixture glows brightly, leaving a grey-white solid containing dark silicon.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium removes oxygen from silicon dioxide, reducing it to silicon. It is a simple laboratory way to obtain silicon from sand.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Do not inhale fine silica dust. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

reactions.observation_en: Red-hot carbon slowly disappears in the gas stream; the gas leaving burns with a blue flame.
reactions.explanation_en: Hot carbon reduces CO₂ to carbon monoxide (the Boudouard reaction). In a blast furnace the CO formed is what actually reduces the iron ore.
reactions.safety_notes: Carbon monoxide is toxic. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away.

reactions.observation_en: Steam passed over white-hot coke gives a colorless gas that burns with a blue flame.
reactions.explanation_en: Carbon reduces steam to hydrogen and is oxidized to carbon monoxide. The CO + H₂ mixture (water gas) is an industrial fuel and source of hydrogen. The reaction is endothermic.
reactions.safety_notes: Carbon monoxide is toxic. Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away.

reactions.observation_en: Steam passed over red-hot iron leaves a black solid, and the gas collected burns with a pop.
reactions.explanation_en: Iron does not react with cold water, but red-hot iron reduces steam to hydrogen and forms magnetite, Fe₃O₄. The reaction is reversible.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away.

reactions.observation_en: Hot zinc glows in steam, forming zinc oxide (yellow while hot, white when cold) and hydrogen gas.
reactions.explanation_en: Zinc is not reactive enough for cold water, but it reduces steam to hydrogen.
reactions.safety_notes: Zinc powder is flammable. Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

reactions.observation_en: On very strong heating the white powder is consumed and zinc distils off as vapor.
reactions.explanation_en: Carbon reduces zinc oxide to the metal. Because the temperature is above zinc's boiling point (907°C), the zinc leaves as vapor and is condensed.
reactions.safety_notes: Zinc powder is flammable. Carbon monoxide is toxic. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away.

reactions.observation_en: The red-brown powder turns grey-black and becomes magnetic; water droplets condense in the cool part of the tube.
reactions.explanation_en: Hydrogen removes oxygen from the oxide, reducing it to iron metal. 'Direct reduced iron' is made this way.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away.

reactions.observation_en: The black powder turns to grey iron and water vapor leaves the tube.
reactions.explanation_en: The reverse of the iron-steam reaction: with excess hydrogen and steam removed, the equilibrium shifts toward iron.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen gas is flammable; keep flames away. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: Once ignited the mixture burns with a blinding white glow and showers of sparks, leaving a bead of chromium metal.
reactions.explanation_en: Aluminium is more reactive than chromium and takes its oxygen (aluminothermic reduction). Chromium is produced industrially this way.
reactions.safety_notes: Aluminium powder is flammable. Avoid inhaling chromium oxide dust. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The mixture reacts almost explosively with a bright flash, leaving molten copper.
reactions.explanation_en: Aluminium reduces copper(II) oxide to copper. Because copper holds oxygen weakly, this thermite is much more violent than the iron one.
reactions.safety_notes: Aluminium powder is flammable. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it.

reactions.observation_en: A brilliant white flash; afterwards white magnesium oxide and red-brown copper remain.
reactions.explanation_en: Magnesium is far more reactive than copper and removes the oxygen from copper(II) oxide very exothermically.
reactions.safety_notes: Burning magnesium is blinding; do not look directly at it. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The hot black oxide turns to pink-brown copper and water droplets collect further along the tube.
reactions.explanation_en: Ammonia acts as a reducing agent: it takes oxygen from CuO and is oxidized to nitrogen gas.
reactions.safety_notes: Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: A hot black copper coil turns shiny pink-red in ethanol vapor and a sharp, fruity smell of ethanal appears.
reactions.explanation_en: Hot CuO oxidizes the primary alcohol ethanol to the aldehyde ethanal and is reduced to copper metal.
reactions.safety_notes: Ethanol is flammable. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: A hot black copper coil turns shiny pink-red in methanol vapor and a pungent smell of formaldehyde appears.
reactions.explanation_en: Hot CuO oxidizes methanol to methanal (formaldehyde) and is reduced to copper metal.
reactions.safety_notes: Methanol is toxic and flammable. Formaldehyde is toxic and carcinogenic. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture.

reactions.observation_en: The white solid slowly gains mass as it absorbs the gas; no other visible change.
reactions.explanation_en: The basic oxide CaO combines with the acidic oxide CO₂ to form calcium carbonate — the reverse of making quicklime in a kiln.
reactions.safety_notes: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The white solid absorbs the gas and warms up.
reactions.explanation_en: A basic oxide and an acidic oxide combine directly into a salt, sodium carbonate.
reactions.safety_notes: Sodium oxide is corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture.
Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The hot white solid absorbs the choking gas.
reactions.explanation_en: Basic CaO neutralizes acidic SO₂ to give calcium sulfite. Power stations use this reaction to remove SO₂ from flue gas.
reactions.safety_notes: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture. Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.

warnings_en: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture.
Do not inhale fine silica dust.

reactions.observation_en: At bright red heat the two white solids fuse into a glassy molten slag.
reactions.explanation_en: Basic calcium oxide reacts with acidic silica to form calcium silicate. In the blast furnace this removes sandy impurities as slag.
reactions.safety_notes: Quicklime is corrosive and reacts with moisture. Do not inhale fine silica dust. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.

warnings_en: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer.
Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The purple color disappears and yellow-green chlorine gas is given off.
reactions.explanation_en: Permanganate (Mn +7) oxidizes chloride ions to chlorine and is reduced to almost colorless Mn²⁺. This is a convenient laboratory preparation of chlorine.
reactions.safety_notes: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: On warming, the black powder dissolves and yellow-green chlorine gas is evolved.
reactions.explanation_en: MnO₂ (Mn +4) oxidizes chloride to chlorine and is reduced to Mn²⁺. Scheele discovered chlorine with this reaction in 1774.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: On warming with concentrated acid the orange color turns green and chlorine gas is evolved.
reactions.explanation_en: Dichromate (Cr +6) oxidizes chloride ions to chlorine and is reduced to green Cr³⁺.
reactions.safety_notes: Dichromate is toxic and carcinogenic. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer.

reactions.observation_en: Each drop of purple permanganate is decolorized at once; the first permanent pale pink marks the end point.
reactions.explanation_en: In acid, MnO₄⁻ oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and is reduced to colorless Mn²⁺ (1 MnO₄⁻ : 5 Fe²⁺). Permanganate is its own indicator.
reactions.safety_notes: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer.
Iodine is harmful and stains skin.

reactions.observation_en: The purple color vanishes and the solution turns deep brown as iodine is set free.
reactions.explanation_en: Acidified permanganate oxidizes iodide ions to iodine and is reduced to Mn²⁺.
reactions.safety_notes: Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Iodine is harmful and stains skin.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.
Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer.

reactions.observation_en: The purple solution is decolorized as the gas bubbles through.
reactions.explanation_en: SO₂ is a reducing agent: it is oxidized to sulfate while purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to colorless Mn²⁺. This is a test for sulfur dioxide.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood. Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidizer. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant.

reactions.observation_en: The liquid froths up violently and gets hot; with detergent a huge column of warm foam shoots out.
reactions.explanation_en: Iodide ions catalyze the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. The catalyst is not used up. The reaction is strongly exothermic (−98 kJ per mole of H₂O₂).
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant. Oxygen strongly supports combustion.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant.
Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia.

reactions.observation_en: Vigorous fizzing as oxygen gas is released; the mixture warms up.
reactions.explanation_en: Hypochlorite oxidizes hydrogen peroxide to oxygen and is reduced to chloride. Here H₂O₂ acts as a reducing agent.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant. Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia. Oxygen strongly supports combustion.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant.

reactions.observation_en: The pale green solution turns yellow-brown.
reactions.explanation_en: In acid, hydrogen peroxide oxidizes Fe²⁺ (pale green) to Fe³⁺ (yellow-brown) and is reduced to water.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.
Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant.

reactions.observation_en: The gas is absorbed with no visible change; the solution becomes strongly acidic and warm.
reactions.explanation_en: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes sulfur from +4 in SO₂ to +6 in sulfuric acid. The same reaction in cloud droplets produces acid rain.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood. Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidizer and irritant. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.
Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: Where the two gases meet, a yellow deposit of sulfur and droplets of water form on the glass.
reactions.explanation_en: A comproportionation: sulfur at +4 (SO₂) and −2 (H₂S) meet at 0. This is the key step of the Claus process for recovering sulfur, and it also happens in volcanic vents.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood. Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood.
Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: A pale yellow deposit of sulfur appears and the green color of chlorine fades.
reactions.explanation_en: Chlorine oxidizes sulfide (−2) to sulfur (0) and is reduced to hydrogen chloride.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989

warnings_en: Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood.
Iodine is harmful and stains skin.

reactions.observation_en: The brown iodine solution is decolorized and a milky yellow suspension of sulfur appears.
reactions.explanation_en: Iodine oxidizes hydrogen sulfide to sulfur and is reduced to colorless iodide.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrogen sulfide is very toxic; use a fume hood. Iodine is harmful and stains skin. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Hydroiodic acid is corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Iodine is harmful and stains skin.

reactions.observation_en: The brown iodine color fades to pale yellow and then to colorless.
reactions.explanation_en: Thiosulfate reduces iodine to iodide and is oxidized to tetrathionate. This fast, exact reaction is the basis of iodometric titrations; starch is added near the end to sharpen the end point.
reactions.safety_notes: Iodine is harmful and stains skin.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The clear solution slowly turns cloudy pale yellow until a cross under the flask can no longer be seen.
reactions.explanation_en: Acid decomposes thiosulfate into solid sulfur and sulfur dioxide. Timing how long the cross takes to disappear is the classic experiment on reaction rate.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Burning sulfur gives toxic SO2. Sulfur dioxide is toxic; use a fume hood.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Never mix bleach with acids at home: toxic chlorine gas is released.
Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia.
Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The mixture fizzes and gives off yellow-green, choking chlorine gas.
reactions.explanation_en: Acid converts hypochlorite and chloride into chlorine gas. This is why bleach must never be mixed with acidic cleaners.
reactions.safety_notes: Never mix bleach with acids at home: toxic chlorine gas is released. Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Never mix bleach with ammonia: toxic chloramine gas is released.
Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia.
Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: Irritating, toxic fumes of chloramine rise from the mixture.
reactions.explanation_en: Hypochlorite chlorinates ammonia to form chloramine, a toxic gas. This is why bleach must never be mixed with ammonia-based cleaners.
reactions.safety_notes: Never mix bleach with ammonia: toxic chloramine gas is released. Bleach is corrosive; never mix it with acids or ammonia. Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood. NaOH is corrosive.

warnings_en: Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood.
Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.

reactions.observation_en: The green color of chlorine disappears and dense white smoke of ammonium chloride forms.
reactions.explanation_en: Chlorine oxidizes ammonia to nitrogen; the HCl formed reacts immediately with excess ammonia to give white NH₄Cl smoke. Ammonia vapor is used to find leaks in chlorine pipes this way.
reactions.safety_notes: Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood. Chlorine gas is toxic; use a fume hood.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.name_en: Sodium Chloride and Concentrated Sulfuric Acid
reactions.observation_en: The salt froths and steamy, sharp-smelling fumes of hydrogen chloride are given off.
reactions.explanation_en: Non-volatile sulfuric acid displaces the volatile acid HCl from its salt. The fumes form white smoke with ammonia.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Hydrochloric acid is corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.name_en: Potassium Nitrate and Concentrated Sulfuric Acid

warnings_en: Nitric acid is corrosive and oxidizing.

reactions.observation_en: On heating, pale yellow fumes of nitric acid distil over.
reactions.explanation_en: Non-volatile sulfuric acid displaces the more volatile nitric acid from the nitrate. This was the historical way of making nitric acid.
reactions.safety_notes: Potassium nitrate is an oxidizer. Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Nitric acid is corrosive and oxidizing. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

warnings_en: Hydrofluoric acid is extremely toxic and penetrates skin.

reactions.observation_en: On warming, colorless fumes are given off that etch glass.
reactions.explanation_en: Sulfuric acid displaces hydrogen fluoride from calcium fluoride. This is the industrial source of HF.
reactions.safety_notes: Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Hydrofluoric acid is extremely toxic and penetrates skin. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: No visible change, but a smell of vinegar appears.
reactions.explanation_en: A strong acid displaces a weak acid from its salt: acetate ions accept H⁺ to form acetic acid molecules.
reactions.safety_notes: Hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Concentrated acetic acid is corrosive.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: CODATA Key Values 1989; NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: On strong heating a colorless gas is given off that burns with a blue flame.
reactions.explanation_en: Heating sodium acetate with solid alkali removes the carboxyl group as carbonate (decarboxylation), leaving methane. It is the classic laboratory preparation of methane.
reactions.safety_notes: NaOH is corrosive. Methane is extremely flammable. Hot apparatus; handle with tongs.
reactions.enthalpySource: Hess's law from standard enthalpies of formation at 25 °C: NBS Tables 1982

reactions.observation_en: The two dry solids turn into a slush, smell of ammonia, and become so cold that the flask freezes to a wet board.
reactions.explanation_en: A spontaneous endothermic reaction: it absorbs heat from the surroundings but still proceeds because entropy increases greatly (solids become a liquid and a gas). The temperature can fall below −20°C.
reactions.safety_notes: Barium compounds are toxic. Ammonium nitrate is an oxidizer. Ammonia gas is toxic and irritating; use a fume hood.

reactions.safety_notes: KOH is corrosive.

reactions.observation_en: The mixture becomes very hot; if water is added to the acid it can boil and spit violently.
reactions.explanation_en: Hydration of H₂SO₄ is extremely exothermic (about −95 kJ/mol). Always add the acid slowly to the water so the large volume of water absorbs the heat. This is a physical dissolution, not a chemical reaction, but it shows the energy change clearly.

reactions.observation_en: The white granules dissolve and the solution gets hot.
